rv.q: This play is a gift, and you'd do well to go and receive it.
The joy of the play is that it is exuberantly funny while arguing that it is possible to dwell in seemingly antithetical worlds.
Natasha Gordon’s debut play buzzes with comic energy and boasts moments of affecting intensity as it portrays a Jamaican family coping with grief.
It's hard to believe that this assured, multi-layered comic play about grief and ritual is the debut effort of Natasha Gordon, actress turned playwright.
Gordon’s intense, moving play pulls the focus tightly on a grieving family, and the mingled strains and comforts that tradition offers.
It marks an assured playwriting debut for actress Natasha Gordon that would be even more assured had she pushed past 100 minutes.
Gordon's writing is generous with chat, and Roy Alexander Weise's sweet-detailed production often raucously funny, with operatic levels of foreboding.
What is lovely about Nine Night is the roll of speeches: delivered tautly by Franc Ashman, explosively by Michelle Greenidge and magnificently by Cecilia Noble.
There is so much beauty and humanity in this mesmerising debut but what’s more NINE NIGHT is a production full of theatrical magic.
Nine Night makes you laugh and makes you cry and ultimately makes you marvel at the rich panoply of the human condition.
Good things will flow from this flawed but often hilarious play.
These aspects of Nine Night touch a chord and go some way to making up for some of the playwright's inexperience.
Stirring conflicts into the pot, Gordon lets drama simmer to boiling point, but it's too easy to spot the stock grief-stricken flashpoints in a play that's as broad as it is big-hearted.
This is a play that is full of spirit, and spirits.

cn.t: Gordon's assured debut warmly explores grief and dual identity through a Jamaican wake in London, mixing sharp comedy with affecting family drama, though some critics wish it ran longer to fully develop its themes.
